title: The deployed Spell is cast on a freshly deployed Tenderly testnet, so the exact production bytecode is executed before anyone votes
content:
A.1.10.2.4.10.4 has the Crafter deploy the Spell on mainnet; A.1.10.2.4.10.5 then requires that "the Spell Crafter... casts the deployed Spell on a **newly deployed** Tenderly Testnet."

The ordering is the point. Testing before deployment exercises a build of the source; casting the already-deployed contract exercises the exact bytecode at the exact address that the Executive Vote will authorize. Any gap between source and deployed artifact — wrong compiler settings, wrong constructor arguments, a stale build — is invisible to the first and caught by the second.

"Newly deployed" closes the other half. A fresh fork starts from current mainnet state, so the simulation runs against the world as it actually is at deployment time, not against a long-lived testnet whose state has drifted. Deployment and simulation being minutes apart is what makes the result predictive.

A Spell is also single-shot and irreversible: it can be cast exactly once on mainnet, and there is no way to try it and observe. Forked-state simulation is the only mechanism that produces real evidence of what casting will do, which is why it sits on the critical path rather than in optional pre-work.

Note what this buys governance specifically. By the time voters see the proposal, someone has already executed the precise contract they are being asked to approve and observed its effects — so the vote is on a demonstrated outcome rather than a predicted one.
description: A.1.10.2.4.10.5 places simulation after mainnet deployment rather than before, testing the artifact voters will authorize instead of a compiled copy of its source.
